title: Flock Tightens the Rules on Its Nationwide License-Plate Network
hook: After dozens of cities cancelled contracts, the biggest police camera company is adding guardrails to a searchable record of where cars have been.
key_points: Flock's automated license-plate readers feed a nationwide, searchable database used by roughly 5,000 agencies.
Officers must now enter a criminal case number before running a search — previously optional.
A mandatory automated audit flags suspicious search patterns for administrators to review.
Flock now recommends keeping data 7 days instead of 30, and lets agencies block other departments from searching by crime category.
The backlash: a Washington Post investigation found 46 cases of officers using the cameras to track romantic partners.
At least 30 cities dropped their contracts in the year to February 2026; the ACLU argues the real problem is searching without prior suspicion.
content_html: Flock Safety's cameras read license plates automatically and pool the results into a nationwide, searchable database — roughly 5,000 agencies can look up where a car has been. On August 13, 2026, MIT Technology Review reported that the company is tightening how officers reach that data, after a year of cancelled contracts and unflattering headlines.
extra_html:
Three changes: officers must now attach a criminal case number to every search (it used to be optional), an automated system flags unusual search patterns for administrators, and agencies get finer control — Flock recommends holding data for seven days instead of 30, and departments can now allow outside agencies to search only for specific crime categories, permitting a kidnapping investigation while blocking immigration-enforcement lookups.

The pressure behind this is concrete. A Washington Post investigation documented 46 cases of officers using the cameras to track romantic partners, and at least 30 cities dropped Flock contracts in the year to February 2026 — a small share of its business, the company notes. Whether new guardrails help is a fair question: when Flock previously asked officers to type a reason for each search, some Oregon officers wrote "hehehe" 20 times. The ACLU's Chad Marlow frames the real issue as scale rather than bad apples — the system lets police search a huge location record without first establishing suspicion of a crime, doing an end-run around the warrant process. It's a useful lesson for any AI-powered system: the safeguard that matters is the one something actually checks.

flashcards.prompt: What does an automated license-plate reader network actually give police?
flashcards.back_html: A searchable history of where vehicles have been — cameras log plates automatically, and Flock's network is shared across roughly 5,000 agencies.

flashcards.prompt: Which change did Flock make to how officers search the network?

choices.text: Requiring a criminal case number for every search, plus automated audits of suspicious patterns
Deleting all historical plate data permanently
Letting the public search the same database
Requiring a judge's warrant before any search

flashcards.explanation_html: Case numbers became mandatory (they were optional before) and an automated system now flags odd search patterns for administrators. No warrant is required.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the ACLU say officer misuse isn't the core problem?
flashcards.back_html: Their argument is about scale: officers can search a vast location database without first establishing suspicion of a crime, sidestepping warrant requirements.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a self-reported 'reason for search' box a weak safeguard?

choices.text: Nothing checks what's typed — some Oregon officers entered 'hehehe' 20 times
Officers can't type while on patrol
The reason field is hidden from administrators
Search reasons are deleted after seven days

flashcards.explanation_html: A free-text field only works if someone verifies it. Flock's earlier reason-for-search requirement was defeated by officers typing nonsense.
